findings.title: Removing the multi-provider failure allows silently picking the wrong crypto provider when orders tie
findings.body: detectProvider() previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath ("Multiple crypto providers loaded ... Make sure only one cryptoProvider available"). It now sorts by order() and silently takes the first. However DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, so if two of them end up on the same classpath the tie is broken by ServiceLoader/classpath ordering, which is not deterministic across environments and builds. Concretely, a FIPS deployment that accidentally still contains the non-FIPS crypto/default jar would no longer fail loudly; it could silently initialise the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider and run outside FIPS mode. Either give the built-in providers distinct orders and/or keep a hard failure (or at least a WARN) when two providers report the same highest order.

findings.title: New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `int order();` is added as an abstract method to the public CryptoProvider interface. Any existing implementation outside this repository (e.g. the copies/implementations in the keycloak-client repository, custom or vendor FIPS providers, adapters compiled against an older keycloak-common) will no longer compile and will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError. Since a sensible fallback exists, declare it as `default int order() { return 100; }` (or similar) so the interface stays backwards compatible.

findings.title: Test only round-trips the new encoder/decoder against itself and uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512
findings.body: test() converts the DER signature to concatenated R||S and back, then only asserts that the two concatenated forms are equal. A systematic encoding bug (e.g. wrong DER length bytes or wrong integer padding) would be symmetric and the assertion would still pass, while the produced DER would be rejected by a real verifier - which is exactly the interop the new provider exists for. The test should at minimum feed the re-encoded DER into `Signature.verify()` with the public key, and/or compare the output byte-for-byte with the existing BouncyCastle-based ECDSACryptoProvider. Additionally the key pair is generated with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` default parameters (P-256) and reused for ES384/ES512, so the long-curve paths (48/66-byte R and S) are never exercised with realistic values; the curve should match the algorithm (secp384r1 / secp521r1).

findings.title: Indefinite-length encoding leads to NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException
findings.body: readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (0x80). readInteger() and readNext() pass that value straight into read(int length), which does `new byte[length]` and therefore throws an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException (readNext can also compute a bogus positive length). The decoder processes attacker-supplied signature bytes, and callers typically only expect IOException for malformed input, so a crafted/garbled signature surfaces as an unexpected runtime exception instead of a clean "invalid signature" error. Reject length == -1 (and negative lengths) with an IOException in readLength()/read().

findings.title: Dead code: two ASN1Encoder writes whose results are discarded
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two throw-away ASN1Encoder instances and write rBigInteger/sBigInteger into them; the results are never used because the returned DER sequence is built from freshly created encoders on lines 117-120. These statements only waste work and suggest a leftover from refactoring; they should be removed to avoid confusing future readers into thinking the encoding is stateful.

findings.title: logger.debugf() called with a dynamically built string as format
findings.body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a runtime-built message (containing provider class names) as a format string with no arguments. jboss-logging will run it through String.format, so any '%' character appearing in the message would raise an UnknownFormatConversionException/MissingFormatArgumentException from a logging call. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` or `logger.debugf("%s", builder)` instead.
